Venezuela, Colombia to collaborate on border security following kidnappings

Reuters

Nov 12 (Reuters) – The governments of Colombia and Venezuela said on Thursday they are willing to coordinate security efforts to combat transnational crime following two recent high-profile kidnappings along their 2,219-kilometer shared border.

Colombia is seeking Venezuelan help locating the wife of a Colombian mayor and an army officer.

• Colombia’s foreign ministry spoke with Venezuela’s government “to coordinate efforts to rescue” Nancy Gomez, the wife of the mayor of the city of Uribia, in the northern-most department of La Guajira, some 30 km (19 miles) from the Venezuelan border

Show Full Article

• Colombian authorities believe she was kidnapped on November 11 and taken into Venezuela in an attempt to evade Colombian law enforcement

• Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella deployed military troops to the area to aid with the search for Gomez, and said the ELN armed group was believed to be behind her kidnapping

• On November 4, a Colombian army officer was kidnapped by the ELN armed group in the town of Saravena, in the border state of Arauca, Colombian authorities said

• Venezuela’s government said it is “fully willing to carry out all necessary coordination” with Colombian authorities on security matters, the Venezuelan foreign ministry said in an earlier statement

• Armed groups, including leftist guerrillas, have historically operated along the border, where drug trafficking and smuggling are common

• Colombia previously accused Venezuela of harboring FARC and ELN rebels in its territory, charges Caracas has repeatedly denied

• Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora on Wednesday said Colombia had asked the US to work with Venezuela to help find the kidnapped officer

• “We are hoping that with this transition happening in Venezuela, there will be cooperation,” Mora said

• Earlier this year, Delcy Rodriguez became Venezuela’s interim president and began governing the country under US oversight after a US military raid captured then-leader Nicolas Maduro and took him to New York to face trial

(Reporting by Reuters; Writing by Iñigo Alexander; Editing by Anthony Esposito and Daina Beth Solomon)

By Patricia Zengerle WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) – US House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called on Thursday for “dramatic change” in the Middle East and reiterated his support for a two-state solution for Israel and the Palestinians.

Democrats’ sweeping victories in last week’s midterm elections could lead to the curbing of US support for its close ally Israel, putting the spotlight on party leaders’ views as they prepare to take control of both houses of Congress on January 3.

Jeffries, a New York Democrat, is expected to be the next House speaker.

Show Full Article

“The status quo is unacceptable, and we need dramatic change. And that looks like, as far as I’m concerned, making sure you have a safe and secure Israel, living side by side as a Jewish and democratic state with an independent Palestinian state that provides dignity and self-determination for the Palestinians,” he said at a weekly press conference.

Next year, Democratic leaders will have the lead in writing bills and deciding what legislation comes up for a vote, although Republican President Donald Trump retains the power to veto measures passed by Congress. It takes two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate to overcome a veto.

Many of the winning Democrats had campaigned against military aid to Israel and the US-Israeli war with Iran, issues expected to get greater scrutiny in Congress next year.

Washington has historically supported a negotiated two-state solution, although the Trump administration has focused on its own plan for Gaza and a broader Middle East settlement.

The steep toll on civilians of Israel’s campaign in Gaza and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s embrace of Trump and other Republicans had already strained decades of bipartisan support for Israel.

Jeffries called for “dramatic change” in the West Bank, Gaza and to the Memorandum of Understanding with Israel, which provides $3.8 billion in US military aid to Israel each year and expires in September 2028.

(Reporting by Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Jonathan Spicer)

BRUSSELS, Nov 12 (Reuters) – NATO will not hold a summit in Albania next year despite previous plans to do so, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said on Thursday.

Reuters reported in June that plans for an alliance summit in Albania next year had been thrown into doubt due to resistance from the Trump administration and dissatisfaction among NATO members with Tirana’s low defence spending.

Speaking in Dublin ahead of a gathering of European leaders, Rama said: “The issue is that there is not yet common position on when the summit will happen, for sure not in 2027.”

Show Full Article

He added: “And in 2028, if it will be a summit, it will be in Tirana.”

NATO has been considering ending its recent practice of holding annual summits, a move that could avoid a potentially tense encounter with US President Donald Trump later in his term.

However, diplomats say the alliance could still decide to hold a summit at short notice in 2026 — but not in Tirana.

A NATO official said on Thursday that “the next NATO Summit will be held in Albania. A decision on the date has yet to be made.”

In a declaration adopted at the June 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, the alliance’s leaders wrote: “We look forward to our next meeting in Turkiye in 2026 followed by a meeting in Albania.”

But in a declaration adopted at the alliance’s Ankara summit in July of this year, leaders said, “We look forward to our next meeting,” without specifying a time or location for a future summit.

(Reporting by Lili Bayer and Andrew Gray in Brussels and John Irish in Paris; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

Zionism is in a deep crisis. Netanyahu is Israel’s biggest liability

The latest Israeli election is seen as a desperate opportunity for Zionism to save itself from the excesses of its isolated leaders.

Manvendra Singh

12 November, 2026 08:25 pm IST

Follow Us:

-->

1

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

Email

Copy Link

Stay updated with ThePrint:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

-->

Z ionism is facing its most serious crisis since Israel’s creation. The ideology that spurred European Jews to mobilise for a Jewish state now faces the limitations of its credibility in a world that values democratic and non-discriminatory principles . The circle of critics and those willing to pull back from unequivocal support for the Jewish state range from the political to the football field, from music concerts to mass mobilisations across time zones and language groups.

The latest Israeli election is seen as a desperate opportunity for Zionism to save itself from the excesses of its isolated leaders.

The political cost of supporting Israel unequivocally even had US President Donald Trump ru l ing the consequences.

Show Full Article

He said , “It’s a bad talking point.” He even suggested further financial aid to Israel would be stopped. He had timed his stunning statement just as polls were opening for the recently held mid-term elections in the US . The electorate of the country on which Israel depends for its diplomatic, military and financial support voted resoundingly against Trumpian politics. From posh campuses to buzzing counting centres, the vote was a veto.

Earlier, both 2026–27 UEFA Nations League group-stage matches between the Republic of Ireland and Israel were moved to neutral venues due to security concerns. While one match took place in early October, the other took place in late September. T hen there was the unprecedented spectacle of Irish players with black armbands, heads bowed while the Israeli national anthem played, and finally skipping the customary pre-match handshakes.

The drama was played out well beyond the football pitches.

Earlier in the summer, similar sentiments were on display at sold-out music concerts, on both sides of the Atlantic. Such feelings were replicated in enormous street marches.

‘Isreal exceptionally dangerous’ The American reluctance to march against Israeli policies has been jettisoned in recent years as global audiences and social media imagery brought home ample doses of excesses committed in the name of security. In fact, mobilisation has been demonstrated on Capitol Hill as well, with civil rights groups lobbying American lawmakers against deepening defence ties with Israel.

In September, 56 groups had issued a letter to the leaders of the US House and Senate Armed Services Committees.

“At a time in which American interests are increasingly diverging from those of Israel, and American public opinion is turning increasingly against unconditional support for Israel, creating new points of influence for Israel in the US defence-technology ecosystem is exceptionally dangerous,” states the letter .

This sharp division over Israel is in fact a replica of fissures within the Jewish state as to the direction it is headed and should go. The global drop in support, or even empathy, for Israel is largely on account of the leadership style of outgoing Prime Minister Ben j amin Netanyahu.

Following the surprise Yom Kippur attack of 7 October 2023, the conduct of the war on Hamas and its attacking allies in Gaza has been discussed and commented upon ad nauseam worldwide. Even as it deeply divided Israel, the application of disproportionate force retains its reverberating impact across the West.

Also read: Israel’s 100 shades of racism are on display in its election

A crisis moment for Netanyahu West is, of course, where Zionism began, both as a social as well as a political movement. And the West is where support matters for Israel, a settler state like many countries in the N ew World. Additionally, the West is where most of the leadership of Israel has come from, until the 28 October elections.

Although Netanyahu’s electoral bloc emerged the largest, it falls short of a majority, and those not in the bloc are not willing to touch it.

Gadi Eisenkot’s greatest appeal at the ballot box comes down to one simple truth: he isn’t Benjamin Netanyahu.

Eisenkot will be Israel’s first non-European Prime Minister in a country with a non-Western majority. Historically, the largest number of Jews resided in Arab and Muslim majority lands, with a sprinkling in countries like India. These communities predate European Jewry and outnumbered them too.

Loosely, sociologically and linguistically, these communities have come to be called Mizrahi, or easterner. A word that came to be coined after the formation of Israel, ie Zionist Orientalism.

Israeli television host Yinon Magal, a prominent ally of Benjamin Netanyahu, sparked controversy by calling Eisenkot a “monkey” of “Mizrahi-Moroccan” heritage being managed by “Ashkenazi elites.”

Eisenkot has a month to be the first non-Ashkenazi Prime Minister of Israel. The crisis of Zionism is also very much within Israel, as such blatantly racist remarks reflect. And now they’re compounded by the fact that forming a non-Netanyahu government requires at least the explicit or tacit support of 19 Arabic-speaking members elected to Israel’s Knesset.

Even though Netanyahu is not acceptable to a majority of members, he tried to rally them around forming a national unity government to keep Arab members from influencing the government. Arab votes for a Zionist government are indeed a 2026 crisis moment.

Manvendra Singh is a BJP leader, Editor-in-Chief of Defence & Security Alert and Chairman, Soldier Welfare Advisory Committee, Rajasthan. He tweets @ManvendraJasol. Views are personal.

(Edited by Saptak Datta)
